# Introduction

## Motivation and Problem Statement

The ride-hailing market is already crowded. Uber, Lyft, FreeNow, Lime, and Tier
compete for the same trips, and current market reports point to ride-hailing,
increasingly paired with autonomous and electric vehicles, as the segment that
will dominate urban mobility in the near term. Our client, a well-established
German car manufacturer, does not intend to watch from the sidelines. It is
building a ride-hailing platform on a fully electrified vehicle fleet and plans
to launch first in the United States, where customers have proven more
receptive to novel mobility business models.

The gap is not ambition. It is operational know-how. The client can design and
build vehicles; it has never run a ride-hailing fleet, and it has never run an
electric one, where charging schedules constrain vehicle availability in ways a
conventional taxi or rental fleet never had to manage. Before it can plan
routes, size a fleet, or choose where to place its first vehicles, the client
needs a working account of how demand for hailed rides moves through a city
across space and time, and no such account yet exists for the market it plans
to enter.

This report builds that account from historical taxi trip data for Chicago,
made available by the Chicago Data Portal and covering trips from 2024 onward.
Taxis are not ride-hailing vehicles, but in a market the client has not yet
entered, they are the closest available proxy for one: metered urban trips,
dispatched on demand, subject to the same weather and time-of-day patterns
that will govern the client's own fleet. We supplement the trip records with
independently collected weather data and, where it adds value, point-of-interest
data from OpenStreetMap, and we analyze demand at spatial resolutions ranging
from coarse census tracts to fine-grained H3 hexagon grids, and at multiple
temporal resolutions, to establish which level of detail the data can actually
support.

Two decisions sit downstream of this analysis and give the report its
structure. The first is where and when to expect demand, at a resolution fine
enough to plan a fleet against rather than merely describe a market. The
second is specific to an electric fleet: how a vehicle should charge at a
driver's home between shifts, given a battery of finite capacity and a
next-shift energy requirement that is not known with certainty in advance.
Both decisions are considerably cheaper to get right on paper, using
historical data and simulation, than after the client has already committed to
vehicles and charging infrastructure. Getting the second one right also
matters for the reason the client chose an electric fleet in the first place:
a fleet only delivers on that choice if it is charged reliably enough to be
available when a ride is requested.

## Research Questions

The analysis that follows is organized around five questions, each feeding
into the next.

1. How does taxi demand vary across space and time in Chicago, and what
   plausibly explains the patterns observed at different spatial units
   (census tract versus H3 hexagons at resolution 7 and 8) and temporal bin
   sizes?
2. Where are the persistent spatial hot spots of demand, and what do
   Gaussian mixture models and kernel density estimation reveal about their
   structure?
3. Can demand be predicted for a specific spatial unit and time bucket rather
   than simply extrapolated from the previous hour, for instance answering
   what demand to expect on a rainy Sunday between 10 and 11 a.m. on the
   outskirts of the city, and how does a support vector machine compare
   against a feedforward neural network on this task?
4. What charging policy should an electric taxi driver follow at home, given
   a charging rate that can be adjusted every fifteen minutes, a battery
   capacity that cannot be exceeded, and a next-shift energy requirement that
   is only known probabilistically at the moment the driver departs?
5. What do these findings imply for the client's fleet operations, and in
   particular, should the client invest in private home charging
   infrastructure or rely on public charging networks instead?

## Report Structure

The remainder of this report is organised as follows.
@sec-data describes the data sources.
@sec-data-prep describes the preparation pipeline.
@sec-analytics presents the descriptive spatial analysis, the
demand-prediction models, and the reinforcement-learning approach to smart
charging.
@sec-conclusion discusses implications for the client and outlines future work.
